title: Darwin Nunez’s Saudi Arabia move has soured. What now for Liverpool’s former £64m man?
content:
If life at Liverpool had grown exasperating for Darwin Nunez, then what must he be thinking now?

His summer move to Saudi Arabia — which earned Liverpool €53million (£46.1m/$62.8m at current rates), plus potential add-ons — was supposed to be a reset, where he could shake off the ‘misfiring striker’ tag that clung stubbornly to him across three seasons at Anfield.

By playing for the kingdom’s most successful side, 19-time champions Al Hilal, he also had the opportunity to regain his confidence and score enough goals to silence the doubters. With time on his side — he had only recently turned 26 when he moved — there was also the chance that form could secure a move back to one of Europe’s elite clubs in due course.

Yet the past six months have delivered just nine goals in 24 appearances, and now he finds himself omitted from Al Hilal’s squad for the remainder of the Saudi Pro League season.

Saudi clubs can only name eight foreign players born before 2003 in their 25-man squads, and Nunez, as widely reported at the end of last week, has not made the cut. Instead, 38-year-old Karim Benzema, a transfer window arrival from domestic rivals Al Ittihad, has effectively taken his place, although Nunez will still be eligible to play in the Asian Champions League. The knockout phase begins next month but he scored twice on Monday night in a 2-1 victory over Al Wahda, cementing top spot in the West Region of the group stage.

His lack of involvement domestically threatens not just Nunez’s hopes of a happy ending to his first season in the Gulf, but also his chances of an impact on the Uruguay team at this summer’s World Cup. It’s unlikely that head coach Marcelo Bielsa would leave his star striker out of the squad, even without a regular run of games at club level, although stranger things have happened throughout the Argentinian’s lengthy managerial career.

In the October friendly fixtures, Bielsa named a small squad full of young players as he began to cast the net further in search of future players. While Nunez remains the senior and most experienced striker in the absence of Luis Suarez and Edinson Cavani, the thirty-somethings who previously led the line for Uruguay, the lack of meaningful minutes in the months leading into the tournament could seriously impact his preparation.

Even for a player who has so often thrived on chaos, being becalmed in this way was not part of the plan when Nunez pushed for a move away from the Premier League after playing a bit-part role at Liverpool, first under Jurgen Klopp and then their current head coach, Arne Slot.

Another Saudi side, Al Nassr, wanted to sign Nunez in January last year, but Liverpool blocked that move, as they did not wish to disrupt their squad when attempting to close out the Premier League title, which Slot’s men subsequently won. When the ex-Benfica player was then granted permission to leave in the summer, it seemed an ideal move to top up not only his bank balance but also his confidence ahead of a huge season.

Yet his record of six goals and four assists in 16 league appearances, while steady, was not spectacular enough to make him undroppable for Al Hilal. The appetite for instant success among the big clubs in Saudi Arabia is ravenous, so when the opportunity came to land Benzema, a former Ballon d’Or winner with Real Madrid, even if he is well past his best at age 38, Nunez always looked vulnerable.

The fact that such a big-money signing can be binned off so quickly is startling but not unprecedented.

Another former Liverpool striker, Roberto Firmino, suffered a similar fate this time last year. When Al Ahli removed him from the squad to squeeze in the new €50million signing of fellow Brazilian Galeno, it was clear that Firmino’s time was up. Just a few months later, he moved to Qatari side Al Saad.

Al Hilal, for their part, will feel that they have little room for sentiment. They are top of the Saudi Pro League and unbeaten after 21 of the 34 games, but only one point clear of Al Nassr (whose star player, Cristiano Ronaldo, has recently returned to their team after a protest at the club’s reticence to spend this winter). Their squad is full of imported talent, with Spanish former Arsenal defender Pablo Mari also missing out on a place for the rest of the domestic campaign, as well as Nunez.

“The decision was difficult, but that’s the job of a coach. He makes many decisions every day, even in every training session,” Al Hilal head coach Simone Inzaghi said in a press conference last week when asked about the cuts. “Nunez and Pablo are good players. I want them in all competitions, but we know the restrictions on registering foreign players. Time was of the essence, and I made the difficult decision. I calmly informed the excluded players of my decision.”

Transfer windows across Europe are now closed, which limits Nunez’s options of a surprise move away, although the MLS deadline in the U.S. is not until March 26 due to that league’s February-December schedule. The most likely scenario, however, is that Nunez sticks around until the summer and then considers options back in Europe after the World Cup.

Should he retain his place in the Uruguay squad, the tournament may offer an opportunity to remind the world of the talent that persuaded Liverpool to spend £64m on him in summer 2022 after 34 goals in 41 appearances for Portuguese giants Benfica the previous season.

He is still relatively young and he possesses qualities that would appeal to plenty of clubs. At Liverpool, his struggle to convert big chances and take on other tactical instructions played a part in his reduced game time, but he did deliver moments of magic that proved crucial. He was popular in the dressing room, too, and while his emotions often weighed heavily, sometimes they sparked him to great heights.

To play just 24 games for Al Hilal and now see his debut season be as good as over after six months is undoubtedly a body blow.

Yet perhaps it’s fitting that the future remains uncertain: unpredictability has, after all, been an integral part of the Darwin Nunez story.
